analysis.one_liner: Taxes 60% of billionaires' pandemic wealth gains to cover everyone's out-of-pocket health costs for a year.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to six House committees and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would place a one-time 60% tax on any increase in wealth that people with more than $1 billion in assets saw between March 18, 2020, and the end of 2020. The money would pay for a year of free health care at the point of service: the government would cover every deductible, copay, and coinsurance charge for insured people, pay Medicare rates for uninsured people's care, and hand out prescription drugs free to the uninsured. It would also freeze insurers' cost-sharing, bar providers from balance-billing patients, and halt medical debt collection for a year.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. resident with health expenses during the year after enactment: insured people would stop paying deductibles, copays, and coinsurance on covered care, including COVID testing, treatment, and vaccines; uninsured people would have their care paid at Medicare rates and receive outpatient prescription drugs at no cost; and people with COVID-related medical debt would get it wiped out and collection halted. Plans would be barred from raising cost-sharing or cutting benefits during the year.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Anyone with health bills or medical debt

how_it_helps.text: HHS would pay all cost-sharing — deductibles, copayments, coinsurance — for people on public or private insurance, and would pay providers Medicare rates for uninsured patients' medically necessary care, for one year.
Uninsured people would get outpatient prescription drugs free, with pharmacies reimbursed at the price the Veterans Affairs Department pays and drug manufacturers required to cover the difference.
Providers participating in the program must immediately halt medical debt collection during the year and can never collect debt for COVID-related diagnosis or treatment.
Health plans could not raise cost-sharing, cut benefits, or become less generous during the program, and providers could not bill patients beyond what their plan pays.

Individuals with net assets above $1 billion on December 31, 2020 would owe a one-time 60% tax on the increase in their wealth since March 18, 2020, including unrealized gains, and the tax would not be deductible.

analysis.who_pays: Individuals worth more than $1 billion, who would owe 60% of their pandemic-era wealth gains; brand-name drug makers, who would have to reimburse pharmacies for drugs dispensed to the uninsured and would lose Medicare coverage for their drugs if they refused; hospitals and doctors, who would have to accept plan rates with no balance billing and Medicare rates for the uninsured; and medical debt collectors, whose collection activity would be frozen. Taxpayers would bear the $400 billion authorized for the program.

drawbacks.text: The tax reaches wealth gains that exist only on paper — it applies to the increase in net assets since March 18, 2020 without requiring anything to be sold — which would force owners of private companies, real estate, and other hard-to-value assets to value everything and could require asset sales to pay the tax.

The 60% rate applies to a person's entire pandemic-period increase, so anyone whose wealth grew past the $1 billion line during 2020 would owe the tax on all of it, and it applies retroactively to gains dating back to March 18, 2020.

The coverage relief is temporary: the free cost-sharing, the no-balance-billing rules, and the halt on debt collection all expire after one year, and providers could resume collecting non-COVID medical debt afterward.

The bill authorizes $400 billion in spending without stating how much the wealth tax would raise or linking the two, and it would require four federal departments to stand up the program within seven days of enactment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit would be immediate and broad — no American would pay out of pocket for a year of care during a pandemic, and COVID medical debt would be forgiven. The main design concern is on the tax side: a one-time, retroactive 60% levy on unrealized gains above $1 billion is administratively difficult and hits wealth that has not been sold, which critics would call unfair to people whose gains exist only in stock or business values, while supporters would call it the point of the bill. The one-year sunset limits both the help and the disruption.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to six House committees the day it was introduced, later to two subcommittees, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Ilhan Omar introduced the bill on August 11, 2020, with seven original cosponsors.

The same day, the Speaker's referral sent it to six committees at once — Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, Oversight and Reform, Veterans' Affairs, Armed Services, and Natural Resources — splitting it by subject matter.
It was referred to the Subcommittee for Indigenous Peoples on September 10, 2020 and the Subcommittee on Health on October 6, 2020, and no further action is recorded.
No hearing, markup, roll call, or floor vote ever took place, and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People with more than $1 billion in assets kept their 2020 pandemic-era gains untaxed, and drug makers, insurers, and providers avoided the new payment and billing obligations. Americans went on paying deductibles, copays, and COVID-era medical bills, which became part of a documented wave of pandemic medical debt.

for.name: Rep. Ilhan Omar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited seven original cosponsors.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Primary committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Richard Neal (D-MA)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral first and never scheduled a markup or hearing; the action record shows nothing after the referral and subcommittee routing.

against.name: Speaker Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to six committees simultaneously, a routing that spread it across jurisdictions, and never brought it to the floor in the remaining five months of the session.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so there is no roll call; the sponsor and all 12 cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republican support on record, in a House of 231 Democrats, 1 Independent, and 197 Republicans.

industries.industry: Individuals with more than $1 billion in net assets
industries.note: A one-time 60% tax on pandemic-era wealth gains, including unrealized gains, ending December 31, 2020, with anti-abuse rules covering trusts and gifts to minor children. Their wealth gains during the crisis were the bill's designated funding source.

They would have to reimburse pharmacies for the gap on drugs dispensed free to uninsured people, and their drugs would lose Medicare coverage entirely if they refused to sign on. The reimbursement benchmark is the government VA procurement price, not the retail price.

The government would pay every member's cost-sharing through their existing plans and bar insurers from raising cost-sharing or cutting benefits for a year. Insurers would keep premiums and their role as the payment channel while bearing no new cost — the bill routes public money through them rather than around them.

Providers would get guaranteed government payment at Medicare rates for treating uninsured patients, but must give up balance billing, charge patients nothing for covered care, and halt medical debt collection during the year.

Providers would be required to immediately halt all medical debt collection, including by third-party agencies, for the year, and to never collect COVID-related medical debt. Their business depends on collecting bills that this program would eliminate.
